dhp60:1: Long is the night to him that watcheth; long is a league to him that is weary;
dhp60:3: Long is the revolution of being for simpletons that know not the Good Law.
dhp61:1: Should a man fail to find a companion who is his better or his equal.
dhp61:3: He should resolutely pursue a solitary course. One cannot be friends with a simpleton.
dhp62:1: “I have sons, I have wealth.” With these thoughts the simpleton vexes himself.
dhp62:3: But he is not his own. How then can sons be his? How can wealth be his?
dhp63:1: The fool who thinks he is a fool is for that very reason a wise man;
dhp63:3: But the fool who thinks he is a wise man is rightly called a fool.
dhp64:1: Even if a fool, all his life long, associate with a wise man,
dhp64:3: He will no more perceive the Law than a spoon the taste of broth.
dhp65:1: If an intelligent man, but for a moment, be associated with a wise man,
dhp65:3: He quickly perceives the Law, just as the tongue perceives the taste of broth.
dhp66:1: Fools of little wit walk with their very selves for enemies,
dhp66:3: Committing evil deeds the fruit whereof is bitter.
dhp67:1: That deed is not well done, of which a man must afterwards repent,
dhp67:3: The fruit whereof he receives weeping, with tearful face.
dhp68:1: That deed is well done the doing of which is not followed by remorse,
dhp68:3: The fruit whereof one receives with joy and pleasure.
dhp69:1: As sweet as honey, thinks a fool an evil deed, so long as it bears no fruit;
dhp69:3: But when it bears fruit, then the fool comes to grief.
dhp70:1: Though month after month with the tip of a blade of kusa grass a simpleton should eat his food,
dhp70:3: Yet is he not worth a sixteenth part of them that have well weighed the Law.
dhp71:1: For an evil deed, when done, does not bear evil fruit at once, just as new-milked milk does not turn at once.
dhp71:3: It follows the doer, the simpleton, to consume him, like fire covered with ashes.
dhp72:1: When to his disadvantage a simpleton acquires knowledge,
dhp72:3: It injures the fortune of the simpleton and crushes his head.
dhp73:1: The simpleton will seek for false reputation, for precedence among the monks,
dhp73:3: For authority in the monasteries, for honors among other folk.
dhp74:1: “Let layman and monk both think that it was I, and I alone, who did this;
dhp74:3: Let them be subject to my will, both in everything that ought to be done, and in everything that ought not to be done!”
dhp74:5: Thus resolves the simpleton; so do his desire and pride increase.
dhp75:1: For one road leads to gain, the other to Nibbāna.
dhp75:3: Understanding this, the monk, the disciple of the Buddha,
dhp75:5: Should not delight in worldly gain, but should devote himself to solitude.
